question.text: An 81-year-old man patient recently moved into an assisted living facility and presents today with itchy blisters in his axilla. He attributes these to a poor diet. He also complains that the nurse practitioner at the facility started him on 4 new medications, in addition to his existing prescriptions. On physical examination, tense axillary bullae are noted that do not rupture with light, gloved touch. On direct immunofluorescence, linear C3 and IgG deposits are seen along the basement membrane. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.F: I don't know or cannot answer

medgemma_4b.clinical_reasoning: The patient's presentation of tense, non-rupturing blisters in the axilla, along with linear C3 and IgG deposits on direct immunofluorescence, strongly suggests bullous pemphigoid. The age of the patient and the new medications also support this diagnosis.
medgemma_4b.critical_evidence: Linear C3 and IgG deposits along the basement membrane on direct immunofluorescence is highly characteristic of bullous pemphigoid.
medgemma_4b.differential_considered: Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome is typically seen in children and presents with more widespread blistering and epidermal detachment. Pemphigus vulgaris presents with flaccid blisters and mucosal involvement, which is not described in this case. Cicatricial pemphigoid can also cause tense blisters, but it is more commonly seen in older individuals and often involves scarring. While the new medications could be a contributing factor, the immunofluorescence findings are more specific to bullous pemphigoid.

rnj1_8b.clinical_reasoning: The patient's itchy blisters in the axilla, which do not rupture with light touch and show linear C3 and IgG deposits on immunofluorescence, strongly suggest a drug-induced autoimmune blistering disorder. Bullous pemphigoid is characterized by tense bullae with epidermal-dermal separation, typically occurring at mucocutaneous junctions, and is associated with linear immunoglobulin deposits. The presence of these specific immunofluorescence findings supports this diagnosis over other blistering disorders.
rnj1_8b.critical_evidence: Linear C3 and IgG deposits on immunofluorescence
rnj1_8b.differential_considered: Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome (A) was ruled out due to the absence of fever and systemic illness, which are typically present. Pemphigus vulgaris (C) typically presents with oral mucosal involvement and larger, weeping bullae. Cicatricial pemphigoid (D) usually presents with erosions rather than bullae. The new medications may have triggered a drug-induced form of bullous pemphigoid.

qwen3_vl_8b.clinical_reasoning: The patient is an elderly man with tense, non-rupturing axillary bullae and a positive direct immunofluorescence showing linear C3 and IgG deposits along the basement membrane — classic findings for bullous pemphigoid. The clinical presentation is not consistent with infectious or autoimmune blistering diseases like pemphigus vulgaris or cicatricial pemphigoid, which typically show intraepithelial blistering and different immunofluorescence patterns. Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome presents with superficial epidermal blistering and is not associated with basement membrane deposits.
qwen3_vl_8b.critical_evidence: Linear C3 and IgG deposits along the basement membrane on direct immunofluorescence — hallmark of bullous pemphigoid.
qwen3_vl_8b.differential_considered: Pemphigus vulgaris (intraepithelial blisters, flaccid bullae, IgG deposits in intercellular space), cicatricial pemphigoid (ocular and mucosal involvement, linear IgG deposits in basement membrane), and staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome (infectious, superficial epidermal separation) were considered but ruled out based on clinical features and immunofluorescence findings.

olmo3_7b.differential_considered: A) Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome (SSSS) presents with rapidly forming, tense bullae that rupture easily and is often acute; B) Bullous pemphigoid usually involves older adults with tense blisters but does not typically show linear C3/IgG DIF pattern; C) Pemphigus vulgaris presents with mucosal and generalized skin involvement with C3/GC deposition; D) Cicatricial pemphigoid is the best fit for chronic, tense bullae in elderly with DIF showing linear C3/IgG; E) is only chosen if no diagnosis fits, but the DIF findings align with cicatricial pemphigoid. F is not applicable here.
